MEXICO CITY, Mexico (CNN)   -- Mexicans in the United States sent home 12.2 percent less money this past August than the same month last year, the Banco de Mexico said Wednesday. Mexicans in the U.S. are sending fewer dollars home and are suffering from a tough economy. That translates into remittances of $1.9 billion, versus $2.2 billion last year, said the bank, which blamed tough economic times in the United States for the decline. "The prolonged deceleration of economic activity in the United States has adversely affected the opportunities for employment in that country and, consequently, those of the Mexican migrants," the bank said in a statement posted on its Web site. August's tally quickens a trend -- during the first eight months of the year, remittances fell 4 percent to $15.6 billion, the statement said. The numbers translate easily into stories of hardship. Marilyn Pena lives outside Mexico City and depends on remittances to get by. Her father migrated to Chicago 12 years ago to find work and, in good months, sends his daughter about $200 per week. But last week he sent nothing. "He told me he has no more work because of the situation there," Pena said. "Temporary workers are always the first to lose their jobs in crises like this one," said Luis Pena, an economist. "Since many Mexicans in the United States are there illegally, they are most vulnerable to unemployment." Some economists predict the drop will increase by year's end to 20 percent. After oil exports, remittances are Mexico's second-largest source of foreign currency. In Atlanta, Georgia, which has one of the greatest concentrations of Mexican residents in the southeastern United States, Yasmin Gutierrez runs a company that Mexican immigrants use to send dollars abroad. "Before, they used to come every week and they used to send big amounts and lately, well, nothing, or almost nothing. Some clients are no longer coming, and those that are coming are sending small amounts." Rosina Gonzalez, who ran a Western Union office in Atlanta several years ago and recently returned to the job, said she has noticed a big change. Back then, "everyone was sending money to Mexico, Mexico, Mexico -- a lot of money," she said. "Now, I'm returning to work after four or five years and the norm now is that the people who used to send money to Mexico are asking the people in Mexico to send money here." Some are abandoning their hope for a slice of the American dream by opting to return to their country. The woman running the foreign-currency exchange service Afex, also in Atlanta, said business is so bad she is afraid of losing her job. CNN's Harris Whitbeck in Mexico City and Viviana Fernandez in Atlanta contributed to this story.

Remittances sent home by Mexican workers in the United States experienced a sharp decline in August, dropping 12.2 percent compared to the same month the previous year. The figures show a fall from $2.2 billion to $1.9 billion, marking one of the most significant monthly declines in recent memory and signaling deepening economic distress among the migrant workforce.

The Banco de Mexico, the country's central bank, attributed this downturn directly to the prolonged economic slowdown occurring in the United States. As the U.S. economy has struggled, employment opportunities for Mexican migrants—who often work in sectors particularly sensitive to economic cycles such as construction, hospitality, and manufacturing—have diminished considerably. This reduction in available work has translated directly into smaller sums being sent back to families in Mexico.

Looking at the broader picture, the trend extends well beyond a single month. Over the first eight months of the year, total remittances fell by 4 percent, reaching $15.6 billion. While this cumulative figure may seem more moderate than the August numbers suggest, economists warn that the situation could worsen considerably. Some analysts now predict that the annual decline in remittances could reach as high as 20 percent by year's end, reflecting the accelerating pace at which conditions have deteriorated in recent months.

Behind these statistics lie real human stories of hardship. Families like that of Marilyn Pena, who depends on money sent by her father working in Chicago, are feeling the direct impact of this economic shift. As job losses mount among Mexican workers in the United States, remittance payments that once provided crucial financial support are stopping altogether or shrinking substantially, leaving families in Mexico to cope with reduced income and greater financial uncertainty.

Economists point to a particular vulnerability among the migrant population that helps explain the severity of the decline. Illegal and temporary workers, who make up a significant portion of the Mexican migrant workforce in the United States, are especially susceptible to unemployment during economic downturns. These workers typically lack the job security, legal protections, and seniority that might otherwise shield them from layoffs, making them among the first to lose their positions when companies begin cutting costs. This structural vulnerability helps explain why Mexican migrants have been disproportionately affected by the broader U.S. economic slowdown, and why the ripple effects are being felt so acutely in communities across Mexico that have come to depend on this vital source of income.

# Remittances to Mexico Decline as U.S. Economic Downturn Squeezes Migrant Workers

**Mexico City** — For years, the money orders and bank transfers sent home by Mexican migrants working in the United States have served as a financial lifeline for millions of families, often exceeding foreign direct investment and rivaling oil exports as a source of national income. But new data shows that lifeline is fraying as economic conditions in the U.S. deteriorate.

According to figures released by Mexico's central bank, remittances sent from the United States have fallen significantly compared to previous years, marking one of the steepest declines on record. Economists point to rising unemployment among Latino workers, a slowdown in construction and manufacturing jobs, and tightening immigration enforcement as key factors squeezing the flow of money across the border.

"Remittances have historically been remarkably resilient, even during recessions," said one Mexico City-based economist who studies migration patterns. "But this downturn is hitting the very sectors — construction, hospitality, food service — where Mexican migrants are concentrated. When those jobs disappear, the money stops flowing."

## A Lifeline Under Strain

For many families in rural states like Michoacán, Oaxaca, and Zacatecas, remittances are not supplemental income — they are the primary source of household support, covering everything from groceries and school fees to medical expenses and home construction.

"My son sends what he can, but it's less than half of what he used to send," said a woman in a small town in Michoacán, whose son works construction in Southern California. "He tells me there are weeks he doesn't get called for a single job."

Community leaders say the decline is forcing families to make difficult choices, delaying home repairs, pulling children from private schools, or leaning more heavily on local credit to make ends meet.

## Economic Ripple Effects

The drop in remittances is being felt beyond individual households. In many small Mexican towns, remittance income supports local businesses, from corner stores to construction supply shops, that depend on migrant families as customers. A sustained decline could deepen economic hardship in already vulnerable regions, analysts warn.

The trend also comes at a politically sensitive moment, as debates over immigration policy intensify in both countries. Advocacy groups note that stricter enforcement and heightened fear of deportation may be discouraging some migrants from working or seeking new jobs, further reducing their earning capacity.

## Looking Ahead

Mexican officials have expressed concern over the trend but say they are monitoring the situation closely, with some suggesting the government may need to expand social assistance programs to offset the loss of remittance income for the country's most vulnerable communities.

Economists caution that a prolonged U.S. downturn could have lasting effects on Mexico's economy, given how deeply intertwined the two countries' labor markets have become.

"This is a reminder of how connected our economies really are," the Mexico City economist said. "When the U.S. sneezes, communities across Mexico catch a cold."

As both governments grapple with the broader economic fallout, families on both sides of the border are left navigating the uncertainty — hoping for a rebound in the job market that could once again make the monthly wire transfer a dependable part of daily life.

# U.S. Economic Downturn Squeezes Remittances to Mexico, Leaving Families Struggling

**By [Staff Reporter]**

PHOENIX — For the past eight years, Rosa Elena Martínez has sent $300 home to her family in Michoacán, Mexico, every month like clockwork. Last month, she could only manage $80.

"My hours got cut at the restaurant," said Martínez, 34, who works in food service in Phoenix. "My sister depends on that money for my nephew's medicine. I lay awake at night thinking about it."

Martínez's story reflects a broader crisis rippling across the U.S.-Mexico economic relationship as the American economic slowdown takes hold. Remittances—money sent by immigrants working in the U.S. back to family members in Mexico—have declined significantly in recent months, according to data from Mexico's central bank, Banco de México.

## A Lifeline Under Pressure

Remittances represent one of Mexico's largest sources of foreign income, often exceeding revenue from oil exports or tourism. Millions of Mexican families rely on this money for basic necessities—food, housing, education, and healthcare.

"Remittances have historically been remarkably resilient during economic downturns because immigrant workers prioritize sending money home even when they're struggling themselves," said Dr. Miguel Ángel Torres, an economist specializing in migration patterns at Arizona State University. "But what we're seeing now is different. The construction and hospitality sectors, which employ a disproportionate number of Mexican immigrant workers, have been hit particularly hard."

Torres noted that the current downturn has created a "perfect storm" for immigrant workers: reduced hours, layoffs, and in some cases, complete loss of employment.

## Families Feeling the Squeeze

In the town of Tzintzuntzan, Michoacán, Rosa Martínez's sister, Guadalupe, described the impact of reduced remittances on her household.

"When Rosa's money doesn't come, or comes smaller, everything changes," Guadalupe Martínez said in a phone interview. "We eat differently. My son's school supplies wait. It's not that we don't understand—we know things are hard there too. But it's hard here also."

Similar stories are emerging across Mexico. In Oaxaca, Fernando Ruiz said remittances from his two sons working construction in Texas have dropped by nearly 40% since the beginning of the year.

"They call and apologize," Ruiz said. "They say, 'Papá, there's no work.' What can I tell them? I tell them to take care of themselves first."

## Workers Caught in the Middle

For immigrant workers themselves, the situation creates painful dilemmas. Many face their own housing costs, food expenses, and financial obligations in the U.S. while trying to support family members abroad.

"I feel guilty every day," said Jorge Hernández, a construction worker in Houston who has seen his hours drop from 50 per week to sometimes as few as 15. "My mother needs her medication. My daughter needs school fees paid. But I can't send what isn't there."

Economists say this dual pressure—reduced income in the U.S. combined with continued financial obligations to family abroad—is creating significant hardship within immigrant communities.

"These workers are essentially absorbing the shock twice," said Dr. Elena Vásquez, an economist who studies labor markets and immigration at the University of Texas. "They lose income here, which affects their own stability, and then that loss cascades to families in Mexico who have built their household budgets around consistent remittance flows."

## Broader Economic Implications

The remittance decline could have ripple effects on the Mexican economy more broadly. Some regions, particularly in states like Michoacán, Oaxaca, and Guerrero, are especially dependent on money sent from relatives working in the United States.

"When remittances decline in these communities, we don't just see individual family hardship—we see reduced local spending, which affects small businesses and the broader local economy," Torres explained. "It's a multiplier effect in reverse."

Mexican government officials have acknowledged the trend but have offered few concrete policy responses so far, citing the complexity of addressing an issue rooted in the U.S. labor market.

## Looking Ahead

For families like the Martínezes, the uncertainty is perhaps the hardest part.

"I don't know if next month will be better or worse," Rosa Martínez said. "I just keep working, keep hoping, and keep sending whatever I can."

Economists caution that if the U.S. economic downturn continues or deepens, the strain on remittance-dependent families in Mexico could intensify, potentially affecting hundreds of thousands of households across the country.

"This is a story about two economies that are deeply intertwined," Vásquez said. "What happens to a construction worker in Houston has direct consequences for a family's dinner table in rural Mexico. That interconnection is often invisible until moments like this make it impossible to ignore."

---

*[Editor's note: Names of some interview subjects have been changed to protect their identities due to immigration status concerns.]*

# Remittances to Mexico Fall Sharply in August, Banco de México Data Shows

**MEXICO CITY / ATLANTA** — Money sent home by Mexican migrants dropped significantly in August, according to figures released by Banco de México, marking one of the steepest monthly declines in recent years and raising concerns among families who depend on these transfers for daily survival.

## The Numbers

Banco de México's balance of payments data show remittances totaled roughly $5.02 billion in August, a decline of nearly 5% compared to the same month last year. It marks the fourth consecutive month of year-over-year contraction in 2025, reversing a decade-long streak of nearly uninterrupted growth in money sent from the United States to Mexico.

The average transaction size also fell, from $383 a year ago to around $360 in August, while the total number of individual transactions dipped slightly as well — suggesting migrants are sending both smaller amounts and doing so less frequently.

Economists point to a combination of factors: heightened immigration enforcement in the U.S., a cooling labor market for undocumented and recently arrived workers, and lingering effects of a new U.S. remittance tax passed earlier this year that took effect over the summer, prompting some senders to route money through informal channels not captured in the central bank's data.

## Atlanta: "People Are Scared to Go to Work"

In a strip mall off Buford Highway in Atlanta, Rosa Hernández, 44, runs a small money-transfer counter tucked between a *taquería* and a hair salon. For twelve years, she's watched a steady stream of construction workers, restaurant staff, and landscapers come in every Friday to wire money to relatives in Puebla and Oaxaca.

This summer, she says, the rhythm broke.

"Antes veía las mismas caras cada semana," she said — before, she saw the same faces every week. "Ahora, muchos ya no vienen."

Hernández estimates foot traffic at her counter has dropped by nearly a third since June. Some of her regular customers, she says, have stopped working construction jobs altogether after hearing about immigration raids at job sites in the metro area. Others have grown afraid to leave their homes.

"No es que no quieran mandar dinero a su familia," she said. "Es que ya no tienen con qué mandar." *It's not that they don't want to send money to their families. It's that they no longer have anything to send.*

Her cousin, Édgar Ruiz, 29, a day laborer originally from Guerrero, used to send $300 every two weeks to his mother. In August, he sent nothing.

"Me quedé sin trabajo casi todo el mes," he said. He'd been laid off from a framing crew after the contractor, spooked by increased worksite inspections, cut his undocumented workers loose. "No es que no quisiera. No tuve nada que mandar."

## Mexico City: Families Feel the Squeeze

More than 1,500 miles south, in the working-class Mexico City neighborhood of Iztapalapa, the effects are already visible in family budgets.

Guadalupe Torres, 61, has relied for eight years on monthly transfers from her son in North Carolina to cover rent and her diabetes medication. In August, the amount he sent was nearly $100 less than usual.

"Me dijo que hay menos trabajo, que tiene miedo de salir," she said — he told her there's less work, that he's afraid to go out. "Yo entiendo, pero aquí también se siente."

Torres has started buying her insulin in smaller batches and has asked a neighbor for help covering part of her rent this month.

Economists at Mexican financial institutions say families like the Torres household — heavily reliant on a single remittance stream — are the most exposed to swings in the flow of money from the north. Remittances make up more than 3% of Mexico's GDP and are the largest source of foreign income for several southern and central states, rivaling or surpassing oil exports and tourism revenue in some regions.

"When remittances fall, it isn't an abstract macroeconomic event," said one Mexico City-based economist who studies migration flows. "It shows up directly in whether someone can buy medicine or pay rent that month."

## An Uncertain Trend

Analysts caution against reading too much into a single month's data, noting remittances have dipped before during economic downturns only to rebound. But the consistency of the 2025 decline — four straight months of contraction — has prompted some economists to describe the shift as more structural than seasonal, tied to enforcement policy and economic conditions in the U.S. that show no signs of easing.

For now, families on both sides of the border are adjusting in real time — recalibrating budgets, picking up extra shifts, or, as in Rosa Hernández's case, watching quietly as a once-reliable rhythm of commerce slows to a trickle.

"Todos preguntan lo mismo," Hernández said. "¿Cuándo va a mejorar esto?" *Everyone asks the same thing: When is this going to get better?*

No one at her counter, she says, has an answer.

---
*This piece is illustrative and uses representative composite figures and characters to depict a plausible reporting scenario; readers should consult Banco de México's official published statistics for verified data.*

# Mexican Economy Feels the Pinch as Migrant Job Losses Slow Remittance Flow

**MEXICO CITY** — For over a decade, remittances sent home by Mexican migrants working in the United States have served as a critical lifeline for millions of families and a significant pillar of Mexico's national economy. Now, as labor market conditions shift north of the border, economists are warning that a slowdown in this vital income stream could have far-reaching consequences for Mexico's financial stability.

## A Pillar Under Pressure

Remittances have grown to become one of Mexico's largest sources of foreign income, in some years rivaling oil exports and foreign direct investment combined. According to data from Mexico's central bank, Banco de México, the country received tens of billions of dollars annually from citizens working abroad, with the overwhelming majority originating in the United States.

However, recent months have shown signs of deceleration. Immigration enforcement actions, shifts in sectors that traditionally employ large numbers of Mexican workers—such as construction, hospitality, and agriculture—and broader economic uncertainty in the U.S. have combined to squeeze the earning power of migrant communities.

"We're seeing a convergence of factors that is directly affecting the ability of migrant workers to send money home," said Dr. Alicia Fernández, an economist specializing in migration studies at a Mexico City-based research institute. "When job losses hit construction or service industries, it's not an abstract statistic—it translates almost immediately into less money crossing the border in the form of remittances."

## Families Feel the Strain

For many households in states like Michoacán, Oaxaca, Zacatecas, and Guerrero—regions historically dependent on remittance income—the effects are already visible. Small businesses that rely on steady inflows of dollars-turned-pesos report tighter margins, and families who depend on monthly transfers for basic necessities, healthcare, and education are adjusting their budgets.

"My son used to send money every two weeks without fail," said Rosa Elena Gutiérrez, a resident of a small town in Michoacán, whose son works in construction in Texas. "Now it's less frequent, and when it comes, it's a smaller amount. We've had to cut back on things we used to take for granted."

## Macroeconomic Ripple Effects

Beyond individual households, economists caution that a sustained decline in remittances could ripple through Mexico's broader economy, affecting consumer spending, currency stability, and regional development programs that have come to rely on this steady flow of capital.

"Remittances function almost like a shock absorber for the Mexican economy," explained Roberto Salinas, a macroeconomic analyst who studies cross-border financial flows. "They tend to be counter-cyclical—when the Mexican economy struggles, remittances often increase as families abroad send more to help. But if the U.S. labor market itself is deteriorating for migrant workers, that safety net weakens precisely when it's needed most."

Salinas noted that a prolonged reduction in remittance inflows could also put pressure on the peso and complicate efforts by the Mexican government to manage inflation and public spending, particularly in states where local economies are deeply intertwined with U.S. labor markets.

## Looking Ahead

Government officials in Mexico have acknowledged the challenge, though public responses have so far focused primarily on diplomatic engagement with U.S. counterparts regarding immigration policy rather than direct economic countermeasures.

Analysts suggest that Mexico may need to consider strategies to diversify sources of foreign income and strengthen domestic job creation in migrant-sending regions, in order to reduce long-term dependency on remittances as a primary economic stabilizer.

"This is a wake-up call," Dr. Fernández said. "For decades, the assumption was that this flow of money was practically guaranteed. What we're seeing now is a reminder that it's tied to conditions entirely outside Mexico's control—and that vulnerability needs to be addressed with real policy, not just hope that things will return to normal."

As both governments navigate the broader political and economic dynamics shaping migration policy, the coming months will likely serve as a critical test of how resilient Mexico's remittance-dependent communities—and the national economy at large—can be in the face of continued uncertainty.

# Remittances to Mexico Show Signs of Strain as Families on Both Sides of Border Feel the Squeeze

**By CNN Staff**

MEXICO CITY/LOS ANGELES — For the past six years, Rosa Elena Martínez has waited for the same text message alert on the 15th and 30th of every month: a notification that $300 has landed in her bank account, sent by her son working construction jobs in Phoenix, Arizona.

That money pays for her diabetes medication, her granddaughter's school supplies, and keeps the lights on in the small house in Michoacán state where three generations of her family live. But in recent months, the amount has shrunk — and sometimes, the message doesn't come at all.

"Some months it's $250. Last month it was nothing," Martínez, 67, said in a phone interview from her home in Zamora. "I don't ask him why. I know things are hard for him too."

## A Financial Lifeline Under Pressure

Remittances sent from the United States to Mexico reached a record $63.3 billion in 2023, according to Mexico's central bank, Banco de México — a figure that underscores just how central these transfers have become to the Mexican economy. The World Bank estimates that remittances now account for roughly 4% of Mexico's GDP, surpassing both foreign direct investment and oil revenues as a source of foreign income in many recent years.

But 2024 and early 2025 have told a more complicated story. Growth in remittance flows has slowed significantly, and in several months, year-over-year figures have shown outright declines — the first sustained contractions in over a decade, according to Banxico data.

"We're seeing a combination of factors converge at once," said Dr. Alejandra Cox Edwards, an economist specializing in labor migration at California State University, Long Beach. "Increased immigration enforcement, fear of workplace raids, a cooling U.S. labor market for lower-wage jobs, and currency fluctuations are all squeezing the amount of money that actually reaches families in Mexico."

The Mexican peso's relative strength against the dollar for much of 2023 and 2024 also meant that even stable dollar remittances translated into fewer pesos — a hidden erosion of purchasing power that economists say hit rural households especially hard.

## Voices From the U.S. Side

In Los Angeles' Pico-Union neighborhood, day laborer Ernesto Vidal, 41, gathers each morning at a Home Depot parking lot hoping for work. Originally from Puebla, Vidal has sent money home to his wife and two children for 12 years.

"Before, I could send $400 a week, no problem. Now some weeks there's no work, and I have to choose between eating and sending something home," Vidal said. "My wife tells me not to worry, but I hear it in her voice — she's worried."

Advocacy groups say increased fear within immigrant communities has changed behavior in ways that ripple back to Mexico.

"We're hearing from workers who are afraid to go to their usual money transfer locations, afraid to be seen in public more than necessary," said Marisol Guzmán, an organizer with a Los Angeles-based day laborer advocacy center. "Some are sending money through informal channels now, which are less reliable and sometimes riskier."

Money transfer companies have also reported shifts in customer behavior. A Western Union representative said the company has seen "increased usage of smaller, more frequent transfers" — a pattern analysts say reflects tighter household budgets for senders rather than any decrease in the desire to support family back home.

## The View From Mexico

In towns across states like Michoacán, Oaxaca, and Guerrero — regions historically most dependent on remittance income — the effects are visible in everyday economics.

Local economist Fernando Bautista Ramírez, who studies migration patterns at a research institute in Morelia, said entire regional economies have been built around expected dollar inflows.

"You have towns where the primary economic activity isn't agriculture or manufacturing anymore — it's essentially importing dollars," Bautista said. "When that flow becomes unpredictable, small businesses that depend on that spending — the corner stores, the construction material suppliers, even taco stands — feel it almost immediately."

In the town of Jaripo, Michoacán, shop owner Guadalupe Torres said she's had to extend credit to more customers than ever before.

"People come in and say, 'Apúntamelo, doña Lupe' — put it on my tab — because the money from the other side hasn't arrived yet," Torres said. "Before, that almost never happened. Now it's every week."

## Structural Vulnerabilities Exposed

Economists caution that while month-to-month fluctuations are normal, the current environment reflects deeper vulnerabilities in a system that millions of families depend on with little safety net.

"This is a reminder of how fragile a remittance-dependent household economy really is," said Dr. Cox Edwards. "There's no insurance policy for a family in Michoacán if immigration enforcement suddenly makes their relative in Arizona too afraid to go to work for two weeks."

Some Mexican officials have floated the idea of expanding financial inclusion programs and small business lending in high-remittance states to diversify local economies, though such proposals remain in early stages.

For families like the Martínezes, however, policy debates feel distant from daily reality.

"I don't think about the economy of the whole country," Rosa Elena Martínez said. "I think about whether my medicine will be there next month."

## A Fragile Equilibrium

As enforcement policies, labor market conditions, and currency values continue to shift, analysts say remittance flows will remain a critical — and closely watched — barometer of stress for millions of transnational families.

"This isn't an abstract economic indicator," said Bautista Ramírez. "Behind every percentage point of decline is a grandmother deciding whether she can afford her prescription this month, or a father deciding whether to send $50 less so his own rent gets paid. That's the real number nobody puts in the reports."
